outputs.L1: For dynamical dark energy cosmologies, we perform a suite of gravitational N-body simulations that achieve percent-level accuracy in the relative matter power spectra at all redshifts. This level of precision is essential for next-generation cosmological mass probes. Our matching procedure reproduces the CMB distance to the surface of last scattering and yields subpercent-level power spectra at \(z = 0\) and \(z \sim 3\). We discuss the physical implications of these results for probing dark energy with large-scale structure surveys.
outputs.L2: We perform multiple gravitational N-body simulations for cosmological models with time-varying dark energy, obtaining relative matter power spectra with percent-level precision at all redshifts. This level of power-spectrum accuracy is required for the next generation of cosmological measurements that trace mass. Our matching method preserves the CMB distance to the surface of last scattering and produces matter power spectra accurate to better than one percent at both \(z=0\) and approximately \(z=3\). We also examine what these results imply physically for using large-scale structure surveys to investigate dark energy.
outputs.L3:
The study presents a set of N-body gravitational simulations designed to model cosmologies with dynamical dark energy and to predict their matter power spectra with percent-level accuracy at all redshifts. Such precision is essential because upcoming large-scale structure and weak-lensing surveys will measure the distribution of matter with unprecedented statistical power. To make full use of these observations, theoretical predictions must be accurate enough that modeling errors do not dominate over observational uncertainties.

A central goal of the work is to provide reliable relative mass power spectra for dark energy models whose equation of state evolves with time. The simulations are constructed so that different cosmological models can be compared in a controlled way. In particular, the study employs a matching procedure that ensures the models reproduce the same cosmic microwave background distance to the surface of last scattering. This constraint is important because the CMB provides one of the strongest anchors for cosmological parameter estimation, and matching this distance allows the simulations to isolate the effects of dynamical dark energy on structure formation.

The results show that the method can deliver highly accurate predictions for the nonlinear matter power spectrum. In particular, the study finds subpercent-level agreement in the relative power spectra at both the present epoch, redshift \(z=0\), and at earlier times around \(z \sim 3\). This demonstrates that the approach remains robust across a wide range of cosmic history, from the era when structure formation was still developing to the current Universe, where nonlinear gravitational clustering is significant.

The need for this level of accuracy is motivated by next-generation cosmological mass probes, including galaxy clustering, weak gravitational lensing, cluster abundance measurements, and other large-scale structure observables. These probes are sensitive to both the expansion history of the Universe and the growth of cosmic structure, making them powerful tools for testing the nature of dark energy. However, their constraining power depends critically on precise theoretical modeling of how matter clusters under different dark energy scenarios.

The study therefore has important implications for future surveys aiming to distinguish a cosmological constant from more general dynamical dark energy models. By demonstrating that carefully matched N-body simulations can achieve percent- and even subpercent-level accuracy in the matter power spectrum, the work provides a framework for interpreting high-precision large-scale structure data. This improves the ability of future observations to detect possible deviations from the standard \(\Lambda\)CDM model and to place tighter constraints on the physical properties of dark energy.
outputs.L4:
The study investigates cosmological models in which dark energy evolves dynamically with time, rather than remaining constant as in the standard cosmological-constant scenario. To test how such models affect the growth of cosmic structure, the authors use N-body gravitational simulations, which follow the nonlinear clustering of matter under gravity across cosmic time. A key part of the work is a matching procedure that pairs each dynamical dark energy model with an equivalent reference cosmology designed to reproduce the same cosmic microwave background distance to the surface of last scattering. This ensures that the comparison is anchored to one of the most precisely measured cosmological observables while allowing the impact of dark energy evolution on structure formation to be isolated.

The analysis focuses on the matter power spectrum, a central quantity for describing how density fluctuations are distributed across different spatial scales. By comparing simulations of the dynamical dark energy models with their matched reference models, the study shows that the matching method can reproduce the nonlinear matter power spectrum with percent-level accuracy over a range of redshifts. In particular, the agreement reaches the subpercent level at both the present epoch, \(z = 0\), and at earlier times around \(z \sim 3\). These results indicate that the approach is sufficiently accurate for interpreting data from next-generation large-scale structure surveys, which will require extremely precise theoretical predictions in order to distinguish between a cosmological constant and more complex forms of dark energy. The study therefore demonstrates both the feasibility and the importance of high-precision simulation-based modeling for using cosmic structure growth as a probe of the nature of dark energy.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise abstract for a paper about N-body simulations of dynamical dark energy cosmologies and their impact on matter power spectra.
counterfactuals.output: We present a suite of N-body simulations of dynamical dark energy cosmologies to quantify their impact on the nonlinear matter power spectrum. Exploring models with time-varying equations of state and matching key background parameters to a reference ΛCDM cosmology, we isolate the effects of modified expansion histories and growth rates on structure formation. The simulations show that dynamical dark energy can produce scale- and redshift-dependent deviations in the matter power spectrum, with percent-level differences persisting into the nonlinear regime. These signatures depend sensitively on the dark energy parametrization and normalization choice, highlighting the need for accurate numerical modeling in interpreting weak lensing, galaxy clustering, and other large-scale structure probes. Our results provide calibrated predictions for forthcoming surveys aiming to constrain the physics of cosmic acceleration.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main findings of a cosmology study that matches CMB distance to last scattering and computes percent-level relative mass power spectra at multiple redshifts.
counterfactuals.output:
The study’s central result is that **cosmological models can be tuned to give essentially the same CMB distance to last scattering while still predicting measurably different growth of structure**.

Main findings:

- **CMB geometric degeneracy:** By adjusting parameters so that the angular-diameter distance to the surface of last scattering is fixed, different dark-energy or expansion-history models can produce nearly identical primary CMB peak positions.

- **Growth breaks the degeneracy:** Even when the CMB distance is matched, the **matter/mass power spectrum** evolves differently because structure growth depends on the full expansion history, not just the integrated distance to recombination.

- **Percent-level differences:** The relative mass power spectra at several redshifts show differences at the **percent level or larger**, depending on scale and redshift. These differences are potentially observable with precision large-scale-structure or weak-lensing surveys.

- **Redshift dependence is important:** Comparing power spectra at multiple epochs helps distinguish models that look similar at \(z \simeq 1100\). The growth history carries information that is hidden in the CMB distance constraint alone.

- **Small-scale/nonlinear regime matters:** Differences can become more pronounced on smaller, nonlinear scales, but exploiting them requires accurate nonlinear modeling of the matter power spectrum.

- **Implication for observations:** CMB data alone cannot fully determine the late-time cosmology if models are allowed to share the same distance to last scattering. Combining CMB with measurements of **growth**, such as galaxy clustering, cluster abundances, redshift-space distortions, and weak lensing, is essential.

In short, the study shows that **matching the CMB distance is not enough to make cosmological models observationally equivalent**: their late-time matter clustering can differ at the percent level across redshift, providing a way to test dark energy and expansion-history scenarios.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a short scientific paragraph describing how N-body simulations can be used to test dynamical dark energy models for future large-scale structure surveys.
counterfactuals.output: N-body simulations provide a crucial tool for testing dynamical dark energy models in the context of future large-scale structure surveys. By evolving the nonlinear growth of cosmic structure under different time-dependent dark energy equations of state, these simulations predict observable signatures in the matter power spectrum, halo mass function, galaxy clustering, and weak lensing statistics. Comparing such predictions with mock survey data helps quantify parameter degeneracies with matter density, neutrino mass, and modified gravity effects, while also assessing systematic uncertainties from nonlinear evolution and baryonic physics. As surveys such as Euclid, Rubin-LSST, and Roman deliver increasingly precise measurements, N-body simulations will be essential for distinguishing dynamical dark energy from a cosmological constant.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a brief research summary emphasizing subpercent agreement in power spectra at z=0 and z≈3 for matched dark energy cosmologies.
counterfactuals.output: Matched dark energy cosmologies exhibit highly consistent nonlinear clustering predictions across cosmic time. When comparing models calibrated to the same background distance or expansion constraints, the matter power spectra agree at the subpercent level at both \(z=0\) and \(z \approx 3\) over the relevant range of scales. This close agreement indicates that, once the cosmologies are appropriately matched, differences in the dark energy sector leave only a very small imprint on the evolved density field. The result supports the robustness of matched-cosmology approaches for interpreting large-scale structure observables and suggests that residual power-spectrum differences are likely below the precision threshold of many current analyses, while remaining relevant for next-generation surveys targeting percent-level or better accuracy.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: In academic style, describe the goals and results of simulations designed to probe dark energy through next-generation cosmological mass measurements.
counterfactuals.output:
Simulations designed to probe dark energy through next-generation cosmological mass measurements aim to determine how accurately future surveys can reconstruct the growth and distribution of matter, and how these measurements can constrain the physical origin of cosmic acceleration. Their central objective is to connect observables such as weak gravitational lensing, galaxy clustering, cluster abundances, and CMB lensing to the underlying matter density field, while quantifying the sensitivity of these observables to the dark energy equation of state, modified gravity, neutrino mass, and other cosmological parameters.

A primary goal of such simulations is to evaluate the statistical power of forthcoming surveys, including wide-field optical and near-infrared imaging programs, spectroscopic galaxy surveys, and high-resolution microwave-background experiments. By generating mock universes with different assumptions about dark energy, simulations allow researchers to forecast how well future data can distinguish a cosmological constant from dynamical dark energy models. In particular, they test the ability of mass measurements to constrain parameters such as \(w_0\) and \(w_a\), which describe the present value and possible time evolution of the dark energy equation of state.

A second goal is to characterize systematic uncertainties. Cosmological mass measurements are sensitive to several effects that can mimic or obscure dark energy signatures, including baryonic feedback, intrinsic galaxy alignments, photometric redshift errors, selection biases in cluster samples, and uncertainties in the relation between observable tracers and halo mass. Simulations provide controlled environments in which these effects can be introduced, varied, and calibrated. This is especially important because next-generation surveys will have statistical precision high enough that unmodeled systematics may dominate the error budget.

The results of these simulations generally show that mass-based probes will be among the most powerful tools for investigating dark energy, particularly when multiple observables are combined. Weak lensing measurements can directly map the projected matter distribution and trace the growth of structure over cosmic time. Galaxy clustering constrains both geometry and growth through baryon acoustic oscillations and redshift-space distortions. Cluster counts provide a sensitive measure of the abundance of massive halos, whose evolution depends strongly on the expansion history and the growth rate of perturbations. When these probes are analyzed jointly, degeneracies among cosmological parameters are substantially reduced.

Simulations also demonstrate that the constraining power of future surveys depends critically on accurate mass calibration. For example, cluster abundance studies require precise knowledge of the relation between observed quantities—such as optical richness, X-ray luminosity, thermal Sunyaev–Zel’dovich signal, or lensing shear—and true halo mass. Synthetic survey analyses indicate that weak-lensing calibration of cluster masses can significantly improve dark energy constraints, provided that shear measurement biases, source redshift uncertainties, and projection effects are controlled.

Another important result is that nonlinear structure formation must be modeled with high fidelity. Dark energy affects not only the expansion rate of the Universe but also the rate at which matter fluctuations grow. Since much of the statistical information in weak lensing and cluster measurements lies on mildly nonlinear and nonlinear scales, simulations are required to predict matter power spectra, halo mass functions, and covariance matrices beyond the reach of linear theory. Hydrodynamical simulations further show that baryonic processes, including gas cooling, star formation, and feedback from active galactic nuclei, can alter the matter distribution on scales relevant for lensing analyses. Consequently, next-generation dark energy studies must either model these processes accurately or restrict analyses to scales where their impact is sufficiently small.

Overall, the simulations indicate that future cosmological mass measurements have the potential to test the standard \(\Lambda\)CDM model with unprecedented precision. They can sharpen constraints on the dark energy equation of state, test whether cosmic acceleration arises from a cosmological constant or from new physics, and assess possible departures from general relativity through comparisons of geometry and structure growth. At the same time, the simulations emphasize that realizing this potential requires rigorous control of observational and theoretical systematics, robust mock survey pipelines, and coordinated analyses across multiple cosmological probes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
